items.title: See the Rare Baby Rhinoceros Born at England's Chester Zoo, an Adorable Boost for Its Vulnerable Species
items.desc: The calf, born October 11, is in good health and exploring a secluded paddock with its mother, out of view of the public
items.text:
Carlyn Kranking | Associate Web Editor, Science
A zoo in England is welcoming an enormous new baby: a greater one-horned rhino. Video footage captured the moment of the calf’s birth at Chester Zoo on October 11, and since then, animal care teams have delighted in watching the baby grow.
“The new calf is gorgeous, big and active,” Emma Evison, team manager for rhinos at Chester Zoo, tells Smithsonian magazine. “Every step of the process so far has been brilliant … and it’s a pleasure to see the calf becoming more confident and curious.”
A post shared by Chester Zoo (@chesterzoo)
It will be a few years before the calf gets its namesake horn, but otherwise, newborn greater one-horned rhinos “come out as almost perfect miniatures of their parents,” Evison says. Their skin folds into plates in a way that resembles a coat of armor, and learning how to inhabit their bulky bodies takes some time.
“For the first few days, young rhinos have to work out how their legs are supposed to operate,” she adds. “There’s a bit of wobbliness.”
The baby is healthy, though its sex and weight haven’t yet been announced. Greater one-horned rhino calves are typically around 99 pounds, per a statement from the zoo, and by the time it’s an adult, the animal will be about six feet tall at the shoulder.
The birth marks the fourth calf born to parents Asha and Beni at Chester Zoo. But after siring the calf, Beni died earlier this year from a sudden illness. “It’s lovely to know that his legacy lives on through this calf,” Tom Garland, assistant manager of the rhino team at Chester Zoo, says in the statement. And Asha “has been a brilliant mum to all her youngsters,” he adds. This most recent pregnancy lasted 15 months.
The greater one-horned rhino ’s scientific name is a nod to the animal’s single keratinous protrusion: Rhinoceros unicornis .
Tracking a rhinoceros pregnancy isn’t an easy task. With such thick skin, rhinos are tough targets for ultrasound machines. But caretakers were able to follow Asha’s reproductive cycle by measuring fertility- and pregnancy-related hormones—like estrogen and progesterone—in her dung.
This technique also showed them when Asha was ready to breed, allowing them to safely introduce her to Beni. Rhinos are typically solitary animals outside the mating season, so knowing when they can come together is helpful for zoo scientists hoping to increase their population.

items.title: Mysterious Mercury is about to get a visitor - after spacecraft's eight-year epic voyage
items.desc: The mission is set to give us our best ever view of Mercury - the closest planet to the Sun.
items.text:
After an eight-year journey travelling almost six billion miles (10bn km), a spacecraft called BepiColombo is about to reach its final destination and get into orbit around Mercury.
It will be entering an extremely hostile environment: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and temperatures can reach a fierce 430C and then plunge to -180C, and it is constantly blasted with intense solar radiation.
Until now, the planet has been little explored but the hope is this mission will solve some of Mercury's major mysteries.
These include uncovering why there is ice in its craters despite its proximity to the Sun, and understanding the mysterious hollows that are dotted all over its surface.
"I think it's a little bit of an under-loved planet in the inner Solar System, but I think that's one of the reasons why it is so compelling," said Prof Emma Bunce, from Leicester University, who is a principal investigator on the mission.
"There are lots of reasons, scientifically, why we really want to understand Mercury, how it formed, how it evolved, what it looks like today, but also how it interacts with the Sun and the extreme space weather that it experiences."
The spacecraft - just seen here - has taken selfies as it has closed in on Mercury
The BepiColombo mission, which is a collaboration between the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japanese Space Agency (JAXA), blasted off in 2018 , launching from French Guiana.
With the spacecraft heading deep into the inner Solar System, it has had to battle the Sun's immense gravitational pull.
So it has had its brakes on for the entire journey, and has also taken a very convoluted path - looping once around the Earth, twice around Venus and six times around Mercury - to slow it down enough to get into orbit.
This journey should have taken seven years, but a problem with BepiColombo's propulsion system meant the already epic voyage was extended by a year.
The final manoeuvre to get into orbit is a perilous one: it needs to perform a 37-minute handbrake turn to be grabbed by the planet's gravity.
If anything goes wrong, the spacecraft could hurtle past Mercury.
A close up view of the scarred surface of Mercury
Only two spacecraft have visited Mercury until now - both Nasa missions.
Mariner-10 flew past the planet three times in the 1970s, and then the Messenger spacecraft arrived at Mercury in 2011 and spent four years in orbit.
But there is still much to discover about this tiny world.
Mercury is only a bit bigger than our Moon

items.title: An Isolated Group of Amazonian Hunter-Gatherers Made a Rare Request for Help From Outsiders, Raising Concerns About Forest Degradation
items.desc: Around 20 members of the Indigenous Awá tribe emerged from the rainforest and received food from neighboring villagers. The group has not made contact with the outside world in decades, so experts say deforestation may have left these individuals with no other option
items.text:
For decades, the Awá , an Indigenous tribe in the Brazilian Amazon rainforest, has lived in almost complete isolation from the modern world. That changed on November 16, when a group of around 20 men, women and children emerged from the forest’s edge.
The Awá individuals, some of whom carried spears or wore necklaces and headdresses, made contact with a government agency that supports Indigenous peoples and the Guajajara , a larger, non-isolated Indigenous group that lives adjacent to the Awá. Both reside in Brazil’s Arariboia Indigenous Territory in the northeast state of Maranhão . Guajajara members captured photos and videos of the encounter, which have been shared by the London-based Indigenous advocacy group Survival International.
The interaction lasted for several hours, Stephen Gibbs reports for the London Times , though the two groups spoke different languages, rendering communication almost impossible. Near the end, the Guajajara shared yams with the Awá, who took the offering and, smiling, retreated among the trees.
However, Guajajara spokesperson Olimpio Santos Guajajara warns this should not be taken as a heartwarming story but as a worrying sign about the sustainability of the Awá’s voluntary isolation.
“We were trying to avoid contact with them,” he tells Brazil’s Globo television network, per the London Times . Since the late 1980s, the national government has followed a no-contact policy regarding isolated tribes like the Awá, allowing the Indigenous peoples to remain away from modern society at their discretion. “Unfortunately, today they felt forced to come and make contact,” Santos says.
Sarah Shenker , head of Survival International’s Brazil office, says the pressures of illicit deforestation, cattle ranching and hunting might be pushing the tribe to its limits, forcing them to emerge from isolation to survive.
“They’ve shown so clearly for so long that they don’t want contact with outsiders,” she tells the New York Times ’ Zane Irwin. “The fact that they’ve come out now does indicate they’ve probably felt forced to. … Because their lives are so intricately related to the forest, it would be impossible to completely separate the pressures on the land.”

Of course, womanhood isn’t all girl dinners and hair-tie heroics. As Quinn Mayhew writes for The Manitoban, the path isn’t “a smooth, paved, yellow brick road.” It’s “filled with witches, flying monkeys and a little dog, too.” Women’s work often goes underappreciated. Microaggressions get brushed off as imagined. And women are expected to move out of men’s way, both literally and figuratively.
Then there are the contradictory standards. As Mayhew points out, women are told to speak up, but also to be polite and not too loud. The list goes on: be confident, but not intimidating. Look natural, but don’t let yourself go. And, of course, smile more.
Some of the challenges are far more serious. Many of us live in fear for our safety. We think twice about walking to our car at night, or even going for a jog in broad daylight. And that fear is well founded. According to the World Health Organization , nearly 1 in 3 women worldwide have experienced violence in their lifetime, whether from a partner or someone else.
In what Mayhew calls “a world that is designed so women fail,” it’s no wonder female friendships can feel like a lifeline. “Nobody understands me quite like my female friends,” she writes, explaining that they’ve “experienced the same oppression from a society that wants us to be quiet.” As it turns out, that instinct to turn to each other when things get hard isn’t just anecdotal.
In landmark research from UCLA, psychologist Shelley Taylor and her colleagues found that while men often respond to stress with “fight or flight,” women are more likely to “tend and befriend”: nurturing their children or seeking social contact, especially with other women. That can be as simple as calling a friend, or even asking for directions when lost (finally, a scientific explanation!).

items.title: 56 Celebrity Encounters That Made People See Their Favorite Stars Very Differently
items.desc: Not every celebrity is a Dolly Parton. Someone who's just a delight to meet, and with barely any controversies. Which is how we end up discovering that there are some truly questionable people in Hollywood. The full list of shady celebrity meetings is in the article.
items.text:
We're not joking when we say A-listers seemed ethereal. In fact, celebrity images were highly manufactured, which also contributed to their eventual downfall decades later.
During Hollywood's Golden Age , major studios like MGM and Warner Bros. controlled almost every aspect of a star's public and private life. They scripted interviews, arranged fake romances, and buried scandals in every way possible to keep their stars looking godlike and untouchable. And boy, did they pull it off.
But then came the paparazzi, and that really cemented the idea that even the mightiest could fall. And that's how the image of Golden Age celebrities slowly but surely began to crumble.
This carefully curated illusion started cracking around 1960 in Rome, when Federico Fellini's La Dolce Vita popularized the term " paparazzo ." Magazines no longer wanted just staged studio photos. Instead, they started paying big bucks for candid, unauthorized photos of stars caught in compromising moments.
And nowadays, it's almost impossible to escape a camera. Back then, not everyone carried professional cameras around to capture candid photos of celebrities simply living their lives. Now, keeping things private is nearly impossible because everyone has a smartphone, meaning they have a device that can capture pretty much anything, even a celebrity's every move.
According to researchers , only about 35% of the population had smartphones in 2011, but in recent years, that number has jumped to 91%. So even celebrities just trying to live their lives can never really feel safe, as pretty much anything and everything they do is likely to end up online.
Never miss a story that brings joy to the world. Add us on Google
Still, hearing your favorite actor or musician's name on this list can sting. They're people we admire, so learning about their awful behavior can hit much harder than if it came from some rude stranger.
And well, this is what's called a parasocial breakup. The term parasocial relationship was coined in 1956 and refers to the one-sided emotional bonds that audience members form with media figures. Studies show these bonds can engage some of the same neural networks involved in real-life social attachments, which helps explain why they can feel so intense and why it's almost impossible not to form them.

items.text:
Cancer undetectable for one in 12 patients in daraxonrasib trial, while nearly all participants’ tumours stopped growing
A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades.
In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib , during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.
Though doctors have said the pill cannot yet be considered a cure, and they do not know how long it can keep the disease at bay, they have said it is encouraging news because it appears it will offer patients more time, even if it does not cause full remission.
Half of all people diagnosed with pancreatic cancer die within three months, and only about 3% of patients survive for five years when the disease spreads to other organs. It has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK and has a similarly poor prognosis globally.
Patients were followed for a year and a half during the trial on average and some did not see the cancer return during this period. Longer studies will be conducted to see if any of the cancers can be put into remission. During the trial, tumours stopped growing in 90% of patients, just over 60% of patients had their tumours shrink or disappear, and for about 8% of patients tumours became undetectable on CT scans.
A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45% of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year.
Dr Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, who presented the findings, said “this is the closest to cure”, adding that he had never seen so many tumours disappear in patients whose cancer had spread.
He presented the findings at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona. “We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival,” he said.
“The median follow-up is 18 months. Just imagine, in an average of 18 months your disease just disappears on the CT scan … that’s closest to complete remission … it’s incredible.”

items.title: This Self-Charging Toothbrush Has Bristles That Generate Electricity to Help Kill Bacteria That Cause Cavities and Gum Disease
items.desc: In a short clinical trial, participants who used the experimental toothbrush reported less plaque, gum inflammation and bleeding than those who used traditional nylon-bristled brushes. However, more research is required to assess the tool's safety and efficacy
items.text:
Researchers in China have reinvented a familiar tool: the toothbrush.
Brushing your teeth is an important part of your oral care routine. Both regular and electric toothbrushes rely on physically scrubbing away bacteria that can cause cavities and gum disease. But a new design, described November 4 in the journal Science Advances , features bristles that generate bacteria-killing electricity when they bend, perhaps providing a long-awaited update to the hygiene tool.
“Toothbrushes have undergone no substantive improvements beyond their mechanical function for about 1118 years to date,” the researchers write in the study. “Conventional toothbrushes often fail to establish an antibacterial environment on the tooth surface, allowing bacteria to recover and recolonize. Here, we developed an innovative self-charged toothbrush that integrates daily tooth brushing with piezoelectric functionality.”
Piezoelectric materials generate electricity when put under mechanical stress, like being squeezed or compressed. In the new study, researchers applied this property to the toothbrush by creating bristles from polyvinylidene fluoride, a material that produces an electrical charge when it bends.
The electricity doesn’t directly zap oral bacteria, however. Instead, the charge creates highly unstable molecules called reactive oxygen species in the saliva. These molecules disrupt the membranes of bacteria in dental plaque —a sticky layer of the harmful organisms, along with food particles and spit.
“The concept is great,” Nicholas Jakubovics , an oral microbiologist at Newcastle University in England who did not participate in the research, tells New Scientist ’s Christa Lesté-Lasserre. “Basically, the mechanical forces recharge the surface, so it’s really innovative. Anything that even slightly improves the way dental care works could have a benefit, because oral disease is just so widespread.” Experts estimate that almost 3.7 billion people worldwide have oral diseases , such as gum disease and tooth decay.
The researchers first conducted lab tests of the piezoelectric toothbrush using two key oral pathogens: Streptococcus mutans , which causes cavities, and Porphyromonas gingivalis , which causes gum disease. The charge-producing bristles killed about half of the cavity-causing bacteria and more than half of the gum disease agent present, while traditional nylon bristles eliminated only about 9 percent and 8 percent, respectively.

items.title: The North Atlantic Right Whale Population Has Shrunk, Raising Concerns About the Future of the Critically Endangered Species
items.desc: The massive marine mammals are dying from ship strikes, fishing gear entanglements and other causes, which is affecting the species' ability to grow its numbers. The animals were hunted to the brink of extinction around 100 years ago
items.text:
The North Atlantic right whale population shrank slightly in 2025, raising concerns about the future of the critically endangered species.
Scientists counted 382 individuals last year, according to new numbers released this week by the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium. That’s a 1.8 percent decrease from the 2024 estimate of 389 whales.
Meanwhile, the number of reproductive females held steady at 73, according to the consortium, which is made up of scientists from the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center for Ocean Life and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
North Atlantic right whales are massive marine mammals that can weigh as much as 140,000 pounds. They spend their winters in the shallow waters off North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia and Florida, where they give birth and raise their calves. Then, they swim more than 1,000 miles north to spend the spring, summer and fall feeding in the food-rich waters off New England and Canada.
They’re one of three species of right whales, along with the North Pacific right whale and the Southern right whale . All three species are what’s known as filter feeders, meaning they use their baleen —flexible, comb-like plates that hang from their upper jaws—to tiny creatures called copepods from the water.
Commercial whalers hunted right whales to the brink of extinction by the late 19th and early 20th centuries, dubbing them the “right” whales to go after because they were relatively easy to kill and retrieve.
All three species have been protected under the U.S. Endangered Species Act since 1970. Still, the colossal creatures have been slow to recover—and their populations remain small today. Right whales can die or suffer life-threatening injuries after being struck by boats or becoming tangled in fishing gear.
“Imagine if you were wrapped in rope that moved as you moved … literally sawing into your body,” Philip Hamilton , a biologist with the New England Aquarium, tells CBC News ’ Leila Beaudoin. “It is really painful. They don’t have arms. The pain is … kind of unimaginable.”
Climate change, noise pollution and oil and gas development also threaten the whales. Rising ocean temperatures are particularly dangerous for the massive animals. As the North Atlantic heats up, copepods are moving toward cooler waters, prompting the whales to follow them into areas where they’re not protected from ship strikes and entanglements.

items.title: This Philosopher Was One of the First People to Donate His Body to Science. Nearly 200 Years Later, Researchers Are Still Learning From It
items.desc: Jeremy Bentham, the founder of utilitarianism, had his corpse publicly dissected and turned into an "auto-icon," a lifelike display featuring his skeleton dressed in one of his suits
items.text:
As a young man, English philosopher Jeremy Bentham vowed to donate his body to science, becoming one of the first people on record to make such a declaration. And he made good on his promise. After Bentham died at age 84, his remains were publicly dissected, then transformed into an “ auto-icon ”—a lifelike display featuring his skeleton dressed in one of his suits, which has been preserved by the University College London (UCL) ever since.
Now, nearly two centuries later, Bentham’s body is still yielding new scientific insights.
UCL researchers recently revisited Bentham’s remains, using computed tomography (CT) scanning to create a detailed, 3D model of his mummified head. They share the process and their findings in a short film called Bentham Revealed .
Born in 1748 in London, Bentham was a precocious child who enrolled at Oxford University at just 12 years old. Though he trained as a lawyer, he ultimately devoted his life to philosophy and writing. Bentham became best known as the founder of utilitarianism , a philosophy built around the idea that the best actions are those that produce the greatest happiness for the greatest number of people.
He applied this principle to a wide range of issues, advocating for prison reform , animal welfare , women’s rights , the decriminalization of homosexuality and the abolition of slavery—positions that were considered radical in 18th- and 19th-century Britain. His ideas inspired the founding of UCL, which opened to students in 1826.
But perhaps Bentham’s most radical act was his decision to donate his body to science. In his will, he bequeathed his corpse to his friend, British physician Thomas Southwood Smith , and asked him to arrange a public dissection of his body. Smith obliged, tasking anatomist Richard Dugard Grainger with carrying out the procedure five days after Bentham’s death in June 1832, according to a university statement . Smith then created the auto-icon, which he kept at his house until 1850, when he donated it to UCL. It’s currently on view at UCL’s student center.
Bentham coined the term auto-icon himself, defining it as “self image” or “self representation.” He hoped to inspire others to follow suit. “He imagined a future where people were making auto-icons to keep their dead relatives around,” Tannis Davidson , who led the recent research and serves as a curator at UCL's Grant Museum of Zoology, tells Live Science ’s Tom Metcalfe.

items.title: A Modern Forensic Investigation Reveals the Cause of Death of a 2,000-Year-Old Body Found in a Bog in Northern Ireland
items.desc: Archaeologists teamed up with a coroner to determine that the "Ballymacombs More Woman" was just 15 to 22 years old when she was beheaded in what seems to be an Iron Age ritual sacrifice
items.text:
After more than 2,000 years, authorities Northern Ireland are making major discoveries in gruesome cold case. A public inquest-style inquiry has determined the cause of death of an young woman from the Iron Age, whose body was recovered in a peat bog in 2023. A coroner’s investigation concluded that she was deliberately beheaded from behind with a bladed weapon.
Hosted at the Ulster Museum in Belfast, the proceeding synthesized findings from an international research consortium led by National Museums NI (NMNI). Although not a formal legal inquest, the hearing applied contemporary investigative standards to examine the evidence behind a death more than 20 centuries ago.
“Finds like this that are women are incredibly rare,” Hannah Crowdy , head of curatorial at NMNI, tells the BBC ’s Eve Rosato. “She’s the first of her kind in Northern Ireland at all. This helps us piece together a part of history that is quite mysterious. To honor her, it’s important to tell her story and bring that to the fore.”
The remains were unearthed in October 2023, when peat workers from Bulrush Horticulture uncovered human bones in Ballymacombs More outside Bellaghy in County Londonderry .
Subsequent excavations recovered further skeletal remains and a woven artifact, though no skull was found. Researchers initially thought the body was male and dubbed the individual “ Bellaghy Boy ,” before forensic testing revealed the remains belonged to a young woman between 15 and 22 years old. She was subsequently renamed the Ballymacombs More Woman.
A post shared by Ulster Museum (@ulstermuseum)
Using micro-CT scanning, digital mapping, 3D imaging and targeted analyses of preserved bone, hair, skin, nails and the woven textile, researchers from nine institutions gathered clues about her diet, health and physical appearance.
Cut marks on the woman’s neck appear to indicate that she was “intentionally decapitated in the bog,” Niamh Baker , NMNI’s curator of archaeology, tells the BBC.
The reason for this decapitation is unknown. “It may be that she falls into a pattern of ritual and sacrifice that took place across northwest Europe in the Iron Age period,” Baker explains, adding that comparable Iron Age male remains found in the Republic of Ireland have been linked to leadership positions.
“Was she a female sovereign?” Baker asks. “Or it may be that it was related to an agricultural or weather issue at the time.”

56 years ago today, a patent on the first computer mouse was presented to the engineer and inventor Douglas Engelbart. He became an internet and computer pioneer at the Stanford Research Institute spearheading the creation of not only the computer mouse, but the development of hypertext, networked computers, and early graphical user interfaces. Engelbart never received any royalties for the invention of the mouse, and later said “SRI patented the mouse, but they really had no idea of its value.” Some years later it was learned that they had licensed it to Apple Computer for something like $40,000.
Described in the patent application as an “X-Y position indicator for a display system”, it consisted of a wooden shell with two metal wheels, and was nicknamed the ‘mouse’ because the tail came out the end.
Engelbart wanted to focus his career on making the world a better place by harnessing the collective human intellect of all people to contribute to effective solutions. He reasoned that if you could dramatically improve how we do that, you’d be boosting every effort on the planet to solve important problems—and computers could be the vehicle for dramatically improving this capability.

This week the Empire State Building was illuminated in gold to celebrate NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft passing one light-day away from Earth.
It now takes the farthest man-made object from Earth 24 hours to send a signal back to NASA headquarters.
“The color gold is emblematic of the gold-plated copper phonograph record that is flying on Voyager,” NASA wrote on Tuesday. “The record contains sounds and images selected to portray the diversity of life and culture on Earth.”
The 12-inch gold-plated copper disc is intended as a message from humanity to any civilization that may encounter it. It includes 115 images, natural sounds, music from different cultures and eras, and spoken greetings in 55 languages.
Voyager 1 was launched in 1977 to study Jupiter and Saturn. It crossed into interstellar space in 2012 and continues to send data back to Earth nearly 50 years after its launch.
On Wednesday, the spacecraft passed one light-day from Earth: the distance light travels in 24 hours, or about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers).
NASA will be celebrating the milestone today because of the very fact that it will take one day to receive the signal sent on Wednesday.
For its part, Voyager seems to have decided to celebrate by relaying that it has a problem: something it has been wont to do of late; though considering its age and the distance it has traveled, it can hardly be surprising.
It was on Tuesday that the Voyager 1 mission team became aware that the spacecraft had stopped sending science and engineering data, though ground-based antennae were able to find its carrier signal.
The presence of a carrier signal means that Voyager 1’s Attitude and Articulation Control computer is doing its job to keep the spacecraft pointed at Earth and that its antenna, as well as its broadcast equipment, still work. The lack of data suggests the issue is with the onboard computer responsible for collecting the data from the spacecraft’s various subsystems, including science instruments, and putting it into the right format to be transmitted to Earth.

items.desc: About 20 percent of people alive today with European ancestry carry at least one copy of the variant, according to a new study. It's associated with a smaller occipital lobe, a region that processes visual information, and up to a nearly 10 percent lower risk of schizophrenia
items.text:
Tens of thousands of years ago, Homo sapiens interbred with Neanderthals , resulting in billions of humans alive today carrying traces of these extinct cousins in their DNA. The bits of Neanderthal ancestry can affect mood, metabolism, disease risk and other traits .
Now, new research suggests one of those inherited genetic variants is associated with a slightly shrunken brain region and lower risk of schizophrenia, according to a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on November 16. The findings further highlight the enduring impacts of modern humans’ trysts with Neanderthals.
“This is a very important variant,” says Davide Marnetto , a computational biologist at the University of Turin in Italy who wasn’t involved in the research, to Michael Marshall at Nature . “Its effect is really one of the most beautiful and strong that I’ve ever seen.”
Neanderthals had larger skulls than modern humans, and they were more elongated front-to-back, hinting at a different brain tissue layout. Evolutionary geneticists Hugo Zeberg and Svante Pääbo , of the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Germany, suspected the occipital lobe —which sits at the back of the brain and processes visual information—had something to do with that distinct shape.
So, the research duo investigated gene variants known to affect occipital lobe size in people of European descent, whose DNA typically contains around 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal ancestry . Then, they looked at which variants were not present in people of sub-Saharan African descent, who have little to no Neanderthal DNA because their ancestors didn’t mingle with the extinct hominins, which evolved in Europe and Asia.
The work revealed a genetic variant that affects the DAAM1 gene, which is linked to brain development. This variant upstream of DAAM1 was seen in all five available genomes —complete sets of genetic instructions—from Neanderthals, the team found. Importantly, it wasn’t present in the two tested genomes from Denisovans, another extinct cousin that interbred with humans. The scientists estimate that about 20 percent of people of European descent carry at least one copy of the variant, reports Science ’s Michael Price.
Pääbo received the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for figuring out how to extract and analyze DNA from 40,000-year-old-Neanderthal bones.

The “sensational” discovery of a cave containing the skeletons of over 100 extinct cave bears has been revealed by local authorities.
Kept secret to prevent looting, the incredible assemblage of thousands of bones will remain tucked away behind iron bars until the spring thaw when an interdisciplinary team of scientists will begin studying them.
Discovered in July by a mountain guide in the Autonomous Province of South Tyrol, northern Italy, the cave sits around 9,100 feet above sea level on the side of an almost sheer cliff.
The guide, Kurt Walde, found the cave in the municipality of Enneberg just above another famous cave called Conturines, the highest in altitude in which cave bear remains had ever been found.
That cave was tragically looted before scientists had a chance to study all the animals that lived and died there. When Walde discovered this new, potentially even greater trove of extinct animal bones, Director of the Archeological Heritage Office, Christian Terzer, began work to construct a metal gate and protective tarp over the cave entrance to prevent similar illegal incursions.
“The logistical challenges of managing this project on a vertical rock face at almost 3000 meters above sea level were enormous,” Terzer said in a government statement.
The team was successful, however, and with winter closing in the site has been locked up until next June, when “an interdisciplinary research project with international participation, in which paleontologists, climate researchers, paleobotanists, speleologists, and specialists in ancient DNA will participate,” Terzer told Die Welt.
“With this safety operation, we are protecting not only an extraordinary site, but also the knowledge it contains. Now the scientific work begins, which will give us a more precise picture of how cave bears lived in the Dolomites,” added Provincial Councilor Philipp Achammer in the statement.
It’s unclear to scientists whether the cave hosted Ursus spelaeus or Ursus spelaeus ladinicus, two species of large bear known from Western Europe that lived during the Pleistocene, and which died out during the last Ice Age.
They were significantly larger than today’s brown bears, reaching more than 11 feet in length and standing 5.5 feet at the shoulder, yet they foraged almost exclusively on plant material. Cooking content can be extremely popular on social media, but watching Toronto-area Chef Maddy Goldberg narrate her made-from-scratch recipes, it suddenly all tastes a little sweeter.
That’s because every Tuesday for years, Goldberg has been donating her time to prepare banquets for 100 people in need out of what she finds at the local food bank.
“POV cooking lunch for 100 people using the random food I find at the food bank,” reads a caption at the bottom of every video.
Far from just making spaghetti and meat sauce, or canned this with a side of canned that, Goldberg uses an arsenal of different techniques and flavors to make restaurant-quality dishes, like a lentil fritter spiced with caramelized onion, cinnamon, and curry powder.
Despite attending university for social work, it was the constant cooking for herself and her friends, coupled with an enthusiasm for the cooking competitions Chopped and Top Chef that baked a love of the culinary arts that saw her change her academic path.
Finding herself in the world of fine dining, she told TODAY , there were career characteristics that often disturbed her.
A post shared by Maddy Goldberg (@maddygoldberg)
“The main rule was, ‘Never run out of anything.’ The worst thing you could do was have to tell your chef you’re out of an ingredient, so you can’t complete a dish,” she says. “ So, we would just throw out so much food, it was insane.”
“I always wanted to volunteer at a food bank to understand the other side of the food system. What happens if instead of wasting the food, we gave it to a charity? How does that work?”
Goldberg would eventually leave the restaurant world in favor of private cheffing so as to make sure she had time and room to volunteer, which she began to do at Fort York Food Bank in Toronto.
A post shared by Maddy Goldberg (@maddygoldberg)
She told TODAY that anyone inspired by her work to help those in need don’t have to cook for 100 people. Go to your local food bank, she suggests, and ask what they need. You might find you already have it in your house somewhere—some jar of spice or a pile of food storage bags you’ve never used.
She now boasts 180,000 followers of her work on Instagram, where her food bank banquet prep videos go back to January of 2025, regularly make their mouths—and their hearts—drool.

Warren Buffett marked another Thanksgiving by converting thousands of Berkshire Hathaway shares into a charitable donation valued at about $5.5 billion.
In a short annual Thanksgiving message released with the donation, the billionaire investor and businessman wrote that the most powerful returns in life aren’t measured in stock prices. “Last Thanksgiving I wrote that kindness is costless but also priceless. A year later, I would only add that it compounds, and at a better rate.”
He converted 6,150 Class A shares into 9,225,000 Class B shares which were distributed to four Buffett family-led foundations. The gift continues his plan to give away essentially all of his shares of Berkshire Hathaway – the company he ran for more than 60 years.
Buffett directed the shares to the Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation , a major funder of reproductive health and Nebraska scholarships; the Nebraska-focused Sherwood Foundation , which supports education, human services, and community development in his home state; the Howard G. Buffett Foundation , which works on global food security, conflict mitigation, and anti-trafficking efforts; and the NoVo Foundation , which emphasizes gender equity, regenerative agriculture, and community resilience.
The roughly $5.5 billion Thanksgiving gift is substantially larger than the approximately $1.3 billion in shares he gave the same foundations last year, consistent with his goal of increasing the size of annual grants over time. He has said he intends to complete the transfer of his remaining Berkshire shares to the four foundations by the end of 2034. ⁠
Buffett also took a moment to thank those who helped him along the way to becoming one of the world’s richest men. “Much of my good fortune has come in the form of people who were kind to me and expected nothing in return. I’m grateful to every one of them,” Buffett wrote.
He left readers with a simple message for the season: Pay it forward.
“This Thanksgiving, thank one of those selfless people in your own life. Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else.”

Her youngest daughter said that she remembers her mother holding their hands down the old mountain path in her childhood, and that now it was “their turn” to hold hers.

She never took to urban life. She missed living on the mountain, and Chinese custom required she return at least once a year in April for the Qingming Festival, or Tomb Sweeping Day.

Ellen Wexler | Writer and Special Projects Editor
In the Bible, God’s will often emerges through natural phenomena. The great flood cleanses the earth of human corruption, while the rainbow symbolizes the divine covenant “between God and every living creature.” For millennia, worshippers familiar with these stories have wondered: What meaning can be found in the movements of storms, seas and stars?
That’s the central question of The Book of Miracles , an illustrated manuscript dating to the mid-16th century. Featuring 167 imaginative paintings, the text begins with episodes from the Old Testament and ends with apocalyptic visions from the Book of Revelation . Between them is a catalog of earthquakes , comet sightings , locust plagues , volcanic eruptions and other events spanning antiquity through the manuscript’s creation.
Now, The Book of Miracles is heading to the auction block, where it’s expected to fetch between roughly $920,000 and $1.3 million. Bidders can vie for the volume during Christie’s Valuable Books and Manuscripts sale on December 10.
“The artists of The Book of Miracles have reinterpreted historical and contemporary sources with apocalyptic panache,” per the lot listing . Illustrations of earthquakes, floods and other natural disasters that occurred in Europe are “among the most energetic, imaginative and colorful illustrations in the manuscript.”
The text was rediscovered in the library of a Bavarian castle about two decades ago. It’s since changed hands several times. After acquiring the manuscript, London art dealer James Faber helped date it to the 16th century. The publisher Taschen released a facsimile edition in 2013.

Christie’s attributes the manuscript to two painters, Hans Burgkmair the Younger and Heinrich Vogtherr the Younger , and their workshops. Drawing on the visual language of classical religious art, Chinese artist Yu Hong constructs dramatic scenes that reflect the instability of contemporary life. In a new exhibition, titled Field of Asura , monumental compositions inspired by European altarpieces anchor the presentation, placing the human figure at the center of an imagined world.
In the titular work, a towering column of bodies swirls through a three-part composition. Some figures appear to be swallowed by the mass, while others float above it on clouds. The title refers to the Asura realm in Buddhist and Hindu mythology, an astral world marked by perpetual battles between demigods and deities. Yu Hong draws on this mythology to reflect the ongoing struggles that define modern society.
Yu Hong looks to centuries of religious painting for inspiration, adapting familiar compositions to address contemporary experiences. Her subjects are often people from her own life, including friends and family members. This personal dimension grounds the fantastical scenes in recognizable human experiences.
Across the exhibition, Yu Hong gives particular attention to the physical expression of her subjects. Bodies twist and stretch across the canvas, conveying emotion through posture rather than facial expression. Many figures turn away from the viewer, shifting attention toward their gestures and physical relationships.
The presentation also includes Night Walk (2023), the exhibition’s only previously completed work. Referencing Pieter Bruegel the Elder’s The Blind Leading the Blind (1568), it depicts a procession moving through a landscape of fire and darkness. The scene evokes a collective passage into uncertainty, extending the exhibition’s exploration of human vulnerability.
By bringing historical painting into the present, Yu Hong creates a visual language that feels both familiar and unsettling.

items.desc: The 1952 painting, "Congreso de los pueblos por la paz," allegedly disappeared from Kahlo's house-museum in Mexico City under suspicious circumstances. Heritage groups argue that it rightfully belongs to the Mexican public
items.text:
Christian Thorsberg | Daily Correspondent
Since it was announced last month that a celebrated Frida Kahlo painting would be put up for auction at Christie’s highly anticipated 20th Century Evening Sale , excitement and intrigue had steadily built.
Experts estimated that Kahlo’s 1952 Congreso de los pueblos por la paz ( Congress of the Peoples for Peace ), would fetch between $2.5 million and $3.5 million, a 52 percent increase from its most recent sale just six years ago. The piece shared the pre-auction spotlight with other high-profile works, including a Wassily Kandinsky masterpiece , a Gustav Klimt canvas and a long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe landscape that was recently rediscovered in a Manhattan closet .
But this week, just hours before the first bids were set to be submitted, Kahlo’s painting was pulled from the sale amid questions of its provenance. The interceding effort was led by a group called Defendamos la Colección Gelman (Let’s Defend the Gelman Collection), which seeks to protect Mexico’s cherished cultural artifacts from illegally leaving the country.
In a statement issued this week, the group says that the painting was included in a 1957 inventory that Kahlo’s husband, the famed painter Diego Rivera , created for the Casa Azul Trust, which left thousands of the pair’s artworks, artifacts and personal items to the Mexican people. If you're a photography lover and you own an iPhone, you probably have some thoughts on the way the camera processes images. items.title: From a Small Island in Denmark, This Man Lived Through the Transition From Hunter-Gathering to Farming 6,000 Years Ago
items.desc: A new analysis of the Rødhals Man suggests he witnessed the Neolithic Revolution in his lifetime, growing up eating mostly foraged seafood before shifting to more land-based, likely farmed, foods as an adult
items.text:
Archaeologists have identified a man who likely lived through the shift from hunter-gathering to farming, a dramatic transition that reshaped human history and ultimately paved the way for modern society as we know it.
Researchers have uncovered new details about the diet, lifestyle and health of the “Rødhals Man,” an indigenous hunter-gatherer who lived some 6,000 years ago in what is now Denmark. The findings, published November 16 in the journal Antiquity , suggest the Rødhals Man witnessed the Neolithic agricultural revolution and seemingly found a way to co-exist with farmers.
Rødhals Man is the name given to a near-complete skeleton discovered in 1956 in a shell midden—essentially, an ancient trash dump—on the small Danish island of Sejerø .
For years, researchers were perplexed by the remains. Radiocarbon dating suggested the man was alive between 3900 B.C.E. and 3800 B.C.E., after Neolithic farmers had already begun arriving on the nearby island of Zealand , and lived during a time when people were starting to eat mostly land-based foods grown and raised by farmers. But his DNA revealed that his ancestry was entirely indigenous—he belonged to the Western Hunter-Gatherer genetic group—and his diet consisted primarily of seafood .
“There was something wrong and it is always when things don’t fit that you may be on the track of something important,” lead author Anders Fischer , an archaeologist at the University of Gothenburg, tells New Scientist ’s Chris Simms.
So, researchers decided to take another look at the remains. Their analysis revealed that the Rødhals Man was between 30 and 40 years old when he died—probably closer to the upper end of this range, based on degenerative changes to his body. In life, he stood roughly five feet tall and was right-handed. He had black hair and dark skin, and there’s a very high likelihood his eyes were blue.
The Rødhals Man shows no signs of having experienced violence, and he appears to have been healthy during the early part of his life. Later, as he aged, he developed inflammation or a vitamin deficiency.
An investigation of his teeth and bones revealed that his diet changed over the course of his life. As a child, he mostly ate creatures like mollusks, flatfish or eels, which he likely foraged from the shallow waters surrounding the island. Starting around age 11, however, he began to eat more land-based protein, in addition to seafood.

items.desc: The project aims to create and restore habitats for amphibians and lizards at sites in Yorkshire.
items.text:
The project aims to create and restore habitats for amphibians and lizards
Ponds are to be restored and freshwater habitats created for amphibians and reptiles at two former colliery sites in South Yorkshire.
The Froglife charity has been awarded nearly £890,000 of Lottery cash to carry out the work in Rother Valley, as well as at sites in North and West Yorkshire.
Kiveton and Dinnington Community Woodlands were originally regenerated through the National Coalfields Programme after the pits there closed in the 1990s.
Sheila Grundry, from Froglife, said staff were "delighted" to work in the area because "freshwater will make a lasting difference for frogs and other wildlife and it's a great way for local people to learn new skills".
The £889,761 investment in Froglife's Coalface to Wildspace project will also help local communities connect with nature, according to the charity.
Dinnington Woodland is one of the sites in Yorkshire which will be a focus of the project
The aim of the project across Yorkshire is to create 48 new ponds, improve 93 existing freshwater habitats and establish new "neighbourhood wildlife corridors" like small ponds and bug hotels.
These "corridors" will act as stepping stones for local wildlife from insects to birds, providing food, shelter and water to improve biodiversity across former industrial sites and help wildlife move between one habitat and another.
Conservationist Andy Goff, project manager in Yorkshire, said the transformation of the sites would be for everyone.
"We want people to engage with the nature that is on their doorstep and wildlife in general," he explained.
"I'm really excited about getting people involved from all over Yorkshire."
The Coalface to Wildspace project is funded by The National Lottery Heritage Fund for the next four years, with Froglife having already run similar projects in the Midlands and Scotland.
Rother Valley MP Jake Richards said the project was important for the area.
"These former industrial sites are an important part of our area's history," he said.
"This project will help transform them into thriving habitats while creating opportunities for local people to get involved."

101 years ago today, Robert F. Kennedy was born. The US Senator from New York became Attorney General during his brother John Kennedy’s years in the White House—and would eventually launch his own race for president after JFK’s assassination. READ more… (1925)
Many of the civil rights initiatives championed by the Kennedy Administration and its successor were spearheaded by RFK, who was also known as “Bobby” .
On the night that Martin Luther King Jr. was shot and killed, Robert F Kennedy delivered the news to the people of Indianapolis, Indiana. Local police warned him that a riot could break out there in the heart of an African-American ghetto. He wrote his notes on the ride over and started his speech without any drafts, delivering it on the back of a Flatbed truck. Although all major US cities experienced riots, Indianapolis remained calm, thanks to RFK’s speech.
63 days after that night, RFK was assassinated at age 42 while campaigning for the Presidency. Since his death in 1968, his wife Ethel raised their 11 children and never remarried. She oversaw the Robert F. Kennedy Center for Justice & Human Rights until her death last year.
75 years ago today, Snowdonia National Park was created by British Parliament as the third national park in the country after the Lake and the Peak districts. It protects a mountainous region in northern Wales of the same name of 827 square miles of myth-shrouded mountains and valleys. Much of the park is undeveloped, but there are also many agricultural activities that go on.
The English name for the area derives from Snowdon, which is the highest mountain in Wales at 3,560 feet (1,090 meters). In Welsh, the area is named Eryri. A commonly held belief is that the name is derived from eryr (“eagle”), and thus means “the abode/land of eagles.”
Snowdonia is one of the wettest parts of the UK, and a part of Snowdonia is the wettest part. Nevertheless it remains well-visited by domestic tourists—3.5 million of whom come to partake in the serious hiking and mountain climbing on offer in the park.
For conservation purposes, the whole of the park is not totally protected as Americans would understand that phrase, but it does enjoy a particularly high number of special conservation designations—over a dozen nationally and internationally. (1951)

items.title: SpaceX Catches the Upper Stage of Its Starship for the First Time, Making the Company One Step Closer to a Reusable Rocket
items.desc: After circling the Earth 14 times, the upper portion of Starship descended to the planet's surface and was caught by a giant pair of robotic, chopstick-like arms. However, the company failed to snatch the lower stage, which it had previously demonstrated
items.text:
On November 14, SpaceX successfully caught the separated upper section of its massive Starship rocket as it returned from Earth orbit, marking a historic step toward the development of reusable rockets.
“That was the missing link,” SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during a livestream of the landing, reports Mike Wall at Space.com . “That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship, and now everything changes.”
The 407-foot rocket launched for its 15th test flight from the company’s Starbase site in southern Texas on November 13. The lower stage, called the Super Heavy booster, separated during the ascent after providing the thrust needed for takeoff. The upper stage, called the Starship spacecraft, went on to complete a roughly 22.5-hour journey, which involved 14 laps around Earth and the deployment of 26 Starlink satellites.
After that, the spacecraft navigated back to Starbase, where a giant pair of robotic, chopstick-like arms captured it.
“Can you believe it?” Huot said during the livestream, reports Marcia Dunn for the Associated Press . “Look at her! Baby, she’s back!”

Not everything happened as planned, however. The company had also hoped to catch Super Heavy , which it has previously done three times, per the AP. This time around, the booster had to be diverted to a splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico because of low fuel. SpaceX is investigating what triggered the issue, according to a statement .
Still, snatching the upper stage is harder than grabbing the booster, since the Starship spacecraft travels higher and faster than the lower stage, according to Space.com . The historic catch brings SpaceX closer to its goal of building a fully reusable rocket. The company wants to build a rocket system that can travel to space and back with minimal refurbishments needed between launches.
“If every time you drove somewhere you had to throw away the car, you’d be [like] ‘wow, that’s a crazy car where you have to throw away after every time you drive it.’ But that’s how it works for rockets,” said SpaceX CEO Elon Musk at the X Takeover 2025 event, reports Matthew Glasser at ABC News .

items.text:
Christian Thorsberg | Daily Correspondent
Ahead of a new exhibition celebrating the portraiture of famed Netherlandish painter Jan van Eyck , a new theory has emerged about one of the artist’s most famous—and deeply puzzling—canvases.
At first glance, the scene in van Eyck’s 1434 Arnolfini Portrait seems straightforward: A man, dressed in black, and woman, clad in green, stand at the center of a lavish room where every detail—furniture, a dog, jewelry, oranges—is placed as though to purposefully highlight their wealth. But a closer look at the space’s geometry offers more uncanny observations. There is no fireplace, as would have been expected, and the ceiling is too low to realistically accommodate the chandelier that nonetheless dangles above their heads. Meanwhile, a convex mirror on the far back wall reveals that the pair are not alone; two figures are entering the room. The man in black lifts his hand, apparently in silent greeting, while a large inscription beside his head reads, in Latin: “Jan van Eyck was here 1434.”
Of all the details in the piece, which borders on the surreal, the identity of the man has been speculated upon the most. The leading theory derives from the 16th century, when inventory records labeling the painting as “hernoul le fin” were interpreted to be the French spelling of “Arnoul fin,” or “Arnolfini,” the surname of a wealthy Italian merchant clan who lived and worked in Bruges, Belgium, where van Eyck kept his studio.
For centuries, many art historians have supported this understanding, considering the piece to be a portrait of some members of that family. Some scholars identify the man as Giovanni di Arrigo Arnolfini, while others think it depicts his cousin, Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini. But now, as London’s National Gallery prepares to open “ Van Eyck: The Portraits ,” an exhibition, a new theory put forth about the canvas potentially turns its meaning on its head.
Writing in the exhibition catalogue , Stephan Kemperdick , a curator at the Berlin Gemäldegalerie , posits that the painting is actually a self-portrait of van Eyck and his wife. His evidence is multi-faceted. He points to the Latin inscription as a clear self-reference and suggests that “hernoul le fin” actually translates to mean something like “a deceived cheat.” He argues that the painting, in the early modern period, would have been received as more of a lewd genre piece than a portrait. Huge strides were made for the Land Back movement on Cape Cod. On October 30, 2026, approximately 126 acres of ancestral land were returned to Indigenous ownership. Given the history of the land itself, the transfer was a particularly meaningful one, more than 400 years in the making.
The land, which overlooks what is now known as First Encounter Beach in Eastham, Massachusetts, is near where the Nauset, who are part of the Wampanoag Nation, first came across a group of Pilgrims who had arrived aboard the Mayflower in 1620. While the name of the beach commemorates this historic encounter, it was also the site of a confrontation in which the Nauset defended their homeland.
The property had been in the care of The Nature Conservancy since 1986 and was recently gifted to the Native Land Conservancy, an Indigenous-led nonprofit organization based in Mashpee, a historic town located on the Upper Cape. Founded in 2012, the organization works to preserve natural landscapes while reconnecting Indigenous communities with their ancestral lands.
“This location holds so many stories that were buried and are ready to be unearthed,” said Ramona Peters, founder and board president of the Native Land Conservancy and a member of the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe.
Earlier this year, the organization also purchased a neighboring 20.4-acre property, meaning that approximately 146 acres of land in the area are now under Indigenous care. The conservation area has been given the name T8nupâhs Uwatuhshât, which translates to “at the turtle’s nest” in Wôpanâak. The name is particularly fitting, as diamondback terrapins return to the area each year to lay their eggs.
Aside from its historical and cultural significance, the land is also home to a variety of wildlife, including the diamondback terrapin and eastern box turtle. The Native Land Conservancy will continue to protect the area’s natural habitats while providing Indigenous communities with an opportunity to reconnect with the land and its history.

items.desc: The 1.7 million gigabytes of data include more than 900 million galaxies, more than 60 million potential quasars and about 15,000 candidates of an elusive cosmic phenomenon that can help scientists understand dark matter and dark energy
items.text:
After roughly 13 months of scientific observations, the Euclid space telescope—built by the European Space Agency (ESA)—has released its first big batch of data. The observations cover an area of the sky roughly equal to 9,500 full moons as viewed from Earth, and that’s just a tiny portion of what the observatory will capture as it builds the largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos.
The contents of the 1.7-million-gigabyte data drop, unveiled on November 12, are astounding. They include more than 900 million galaxies; more than 60 million potential quasars , the bright cores of faraway galaxies; and about 15,000 candidates of an elusive phenomenon called strong gravitational lensing , which can help shed light on a cosmic mystery: the dark universe.
Euclid launched in July 2023 to journey to a spot nearly one million miles from Earth called Lagrange Point 2 , joining NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope. ESA’s instrument aims to investigate two mysterious, invisible things : dark matter, which acts as cosmic glue, and dark energy, thought to be behind the universe’s accelerating expansion. Scientists suspect that together, they make up 95 percent of the universe , but neither can be measured directly. That’s why scientists are excited about the thousands of strong gravitational lensing candidates in this batch of data.
Did you know? Another Lagrange Point 2 buddy
NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is currently en route to the second Lagrange point, where it will search for exoplanets and help unravel the mysteries of dark matter and dark energy.
Gravitational lensing occurs when light from a distant galaxy gets distorted by a galaxy between it and the light detector—in this case, Euclid. The way the light gets warped around the obstacle allows researchers to indirectly investigate the dark universe.
“How strongly the light is bent tells us how much matter a galaxy contains, including invisible components like dark matter. With thousands of lenses, we can study how dark ​matter is spread through galaxies and understand how galaxies form and evolve over cosmic time,” Natalie Lines , an astrophysicist at the University of Portsmouth in England and Euclid team member, tells Reuters ’ Will Dunham.

items.text:
Pierre before cataract surgery at Chimp Haven.
The world’s largest chimpanzee sanctuary, Chimp Haven in Louisiana, has performed its first successful cataract removal operation on one of its residents.
Pierre the chimp has long been the alpha of his social group. So when keepers noticed him withdrawing, they knew he was having trouble with his eyesight, eventually going completely blind. Originally from a research laboratory in New York, Pierre had built a reputation as a friendly and inviting presence within his social group who was quick to welcome any newcomers and help them settle into the troop.
But as his cataracts progressed, his daily routines changed. Instead of spending time with the other chimpanzees, Pierre began keeping to himself. He stopped moving around as much and increasingly relied on his hands to feel his way through his surroundings. His caregivers initially suspected he was struggling with his vision, and over the next year he became completely blind.
Over that year, Chimp Haven's care team worked closely with Dr. Kenneth Pierce, a veterinary ophthalmologist, to determine whether Pierre was a suitable candidate for cataract surgery. Pierre passed every test with flying colors and was cleared for the procedure. The operation went well, and he proved to be an excellent patient throughout both surgery and recovery.
But the surgery was only one step in the healing process. Since regaining his eyesight, Pierre returned to climbing and moving around comfortably. He can once again recognize his caregivers and navigate his surroundings without relying on touch to guide him. After spending roughly a year unable to see, he also needed to reconnect with the chimpanzees in his social group.
Reintroduction went smoothly, and Pierre's troop was excited to see him back to his normal self. His caregivers have even noticed behaviors they had not seen from him in quite some time. He no longer carries the weight of being the group’s alpha male, giving him a chance to enjoy life without the demands of leading his troop. Pierre will continue to live his best life with his troopmates and caregivers to watch over him.

items.title: For the First Time, Astronomers Witnessed a Giant Star Gobble Up Its Smaller Stellar Companion
items.desc: The merger caused an eruption in late 2025, which researchers rushed to document using several ground- and space-based telescopes. With older data and the help of computer simulations, the team reconstructed the entire astrophysical process
items.text:
In 2023, astronomers realized that a red giant star in our neighboring Andromeda galaxy was doing something strange. Sure enough, two years later, the astronomical object exploded.
The researchers rushed to observe the phenomenon, and they sifted through older data to piece together what had happened. Analyses suggest the huge star had gobbled up its smaller stellar companion, marking the first direct observation of this kind of star merger. The findings were described November 18 in the journal Nature .
The eruption, called AT 2025abao, occurred because the two stars shared what’s called a common envelope. Some stars approaching the end of their lives balloon to a huge size, entering a giant phase. As an object expands , its outer layer of gas—or envelope—engulfs anything orbiting it, resulting in odd interactions.
However, common envelopes are tough to observe because they happen over relatively short timescales of months to years, and usually, just a few stars exist in this phase at a time within a galaxy, writes Jason Nordhaus , an astrophysicist at the Rochester Institute of Technology who did not participate in the work, in commentary accompanying the study.
Experts estimate that nearly a third of all stars go through a common envelope phase at some point during their lives, reports New Scientist.
To investigate the strange event, which occurred in October 2025, researchers obtained data captured just 47 days later by NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope . They also had follow-up observations from other ground- and space-based instruments, as well as data from roughly the past 30 years, which revealed the big star had started brightening in 2018.

items.text:
A landmark painting by Harlem Renaissance artist Aaron Douglas, titled Harriet Tubman (1931), went up for sale at Sotheby’s Modern Art auction in New York. It carried an estimate of $2.5 million to $3.5 million, the highest auction estimate ever assigned to a work by Douglas. On the evening of Nov. 18, the painting officially set a new sales record for Douglas, but it was far greater than expected; the monumental artwork sold for $14.48 million.
Commissioned by Chicago philanthropist Alfred K. Stern, Harriet Tubman originally hung in Bennett College’s dining hall. The 6-foot-wide composition portrays the abolitionist standing atop a mound of earth as she breaks the chains of bondage. Behind her, liberated figures move toward a new future. Other details show a man cultivating land and a young woman reading, emphasizing the possibilities of freedom, education, and self-determination.
Douglas’ paintings rarely appear on the auction market, making the upcoming Sotheby’s sale particularly significant. The estimate for Harriet Tubman represented a substantial increase. Its monumental scale, historical subject, and connection to the Harlem Renaissance made it an especially notable offering.
Although Douglas created the painting for Bennett College, the work has spent approximately two decades on loan to the North Carolina Museum of Art. The college lacks its own museum and ultimately determined that selling the painting would allow it to invest in other institutional priorities.
Bennett College, a historically Black women’s college in Greensboro, North Carolina, sold the painting to support its future. The proceeds will help fund the institution’s Women’s Health Initiative, which addresses disparities in women’s healthcare. The decision reflects the college’s efforts to preserve its legacy while investing in its students and long-term mission.

In 1967, 33 Massachusetts schoolchildren were given a project: write a letter to a Navy corpsman they had never met who was wounded in Vietnam.
None of them had any idea of the impact their letters had on the veteran, until his son, almost 50 years later, began searching them out.
“I just needed to get back to them and be like, ‘Hey, I know it seems really silly, you’re talking about your pet lizard and you’re saying God bless you, but it made a difference,'” Dave Jacobson tells GNN.
Dave’s father was HM3 Russell Jacobson, who suffered 12 gunshot wounds and shrapnel from a grenade blast. He had been brought home to an understaffed Chelsea Naval Hospital and put in a full-body cast.
Outside, protestors against the Vietnam war heaped abuse on returning servicemen, and for Russell, who Dave described as entering the war as a “pacifist” with the aim of “healing people,” there was a sense of shame, which together with his injuries, began to seep into his very soul.
“He was non-verbal for many weeks and he was refusing food and water, and was down to about 80 pounds. He had lost a dozen of his friends in a couple of hours,” Dave, who wouldn’t be born for another 10 years, explained.
“My mom was a nurse and one of her co-workers was named Kitty. She was always kind of like grasping at straws, like ‘How can we to get this guy back on his feet?'”
“Her sister was a nun at a Catholic school in Gloucester, and she made all the kids write these letters of support.”
It wasn’t as if his father hadn’t been receiving letters: he had, from friends and colleagues, all of whom wrote “kind of what they think they should say.” But it was when Corpsman Russell opened the envelope of 33 letters from St. Ann School and began to leaf through them that, as Kitty said, he began to get back onto his feet.
Slowly, Russell and his wife began to read through the letters, each sealed with a small yearbook-style photo of the author. A boy named Peter talks about his pet lizard, two others talk about how crazy it was that Peter brought his lizard to school. Another asks, as if on the phone, whether Russell knew what was going on with the Montreal Expos’ season.

items.title: Teeth Discovered in Two Chinese Caves Are Rewriting the Story of Homo Erectus, an Ancient Human Ancestor That May Have Been More Capable Than We Thought
items.desc: One new study suggests that the species persisted in mainland Asia for 216,000 years longer than previously thought. Another says Homo erectus was capable of living in a tropical rainforest, a discovery that turns a common extinction theory "on its head," according to one researcher
items.text:
Homo erectus was thought to have disappeared from mainland Asia roughly 400,000 years ago. But newly discovered fossils suggest that the species survived there for much longer, possibly living in southern China as recently as 184,000 years ago. The fossils also show for the first time that H. erectus was capable of living in a tropical rainforest environment.
The findings, described in two new papers published in the journal Nature , are based on recent analyses of H. erectus teeth. One paper finds that H. erectus persisted on mainland Asia for up to 216,000 years longer than previously thought, while the other indicates that the species was even more ecologically flexible than scientists assumed.
Scientists think H. erectus arose in Africa about 1.89 million years ago. It’s believed to be the first hominin species to have spread beyond the continent, with populations reaching what is now Georgia, on the border between Europe and Asia, by about 1.8 million years ago. The species continued spreading east into what is now China, eventually reaching the Indonesian island of Java.
Eugène Dubois , a Dutch anatomist and geologist, made the first discovery of an H. erectus fossil, in the early 1890s. He unearthed a skullcap and femur belonging to the so-called Java Man on the eponymous island.
H. erectus had a more modern, humanlike body than earlier hominins, with long legs and short arms suited to walking and running over long distances. The species made increasingly sophisticated stone tools, probably used fire , and hunted and butchered big game .
Scientists were excavating two limestone caves, located about nine miles apart in China’s Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region , when they stumbled upon nine hominin teeth. They used computed tomography (CT) scanning and physical examinations to investigate the teeth, ultimately determining that eight belonged to H. erectus . The identity of the ninth tooth, however, remains unknown.
Researchers also recovered ancient protein from five of the teeth, including the mystery tooth. In the four H. erectus teeth, they found a version of a protein called ameloblastin that had only previously been seen in older Asian H. erectus fossils.

Johan Rockström, one of world’s leading climate experts, says slowing down scientific work puts cooperation at risk
Climate science is “foundational” to the Paris agreement and worldwide progress on tackling global heating, and attempts to delay new scientific reports threaten global cooperation on tackling the crisis, one of the world’s leading climate scientists has warned.
Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, must be allowed to work as quickly as possible on its next comprehensive assessment of global knowledge of the climate systems .
Some countries are holding up work on the three-part report in a row over the body’s role and representation of developing countries. One group has argued that racist assumptions underpin some of the body’s recommendations.
Rockström said the reports were fair. “The IPCC is objective, evidence-based science, and it’s the only thing that we can reliably stand on as a basis for our policymaking,” he said. “The IPCC is the summary of everything done voluntarily by scientists from the entire world, global south and global north, that collectively carries out a synthesis [of established research].”
The IPCC’s work is used to inform the annual climate “conference of the parties” (Cop) to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. Its next assessment, called AR7, the seventh in a series dating back to 1988, under way, and it is hoped it will be completed in 2028. In the autumn of that year, nations will gather for Cop33, where the second “global stocktake” under the Paris agreement will be thrashed out.
This is the mechanism by which progress towards the core Paris goal, of limiting temperature rises to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels, will be judged. The stocktake is almost certain to find that current pledges to cut greenhouse gas emissions are inadequate and must be improved.
The UN has already found the world to be on track for a 2.8C temperature rise , a level previous IPCC reports have found would result in severe and, in some cases, irreversible consequences, such as the melting of ice caps and glaciers, sea level rises, coral bleaching and extreme weather.
